newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Impact of freed India sugar exports seen muted-ISO.
newsitem.headline: Impact of freed India sugar exports seen muted-ISO.

text.p: The impact of the recent liberalisation of the Indian sugar export market on world trade and prices is likely to be minimal, the International Sugar Organization (ISO) said on Thursday.

Fears that the massive eight million tonnes of white stocks held by India at the start of the 1996/97 crop year will flood global markets have subsided in the past few months, the ISO said in a paper read at its council meeting in Mauritius.

"This is because early expectations of a further production decline (in India) in 1997/98, if realised, would mean stocks would need to be depleted in order to meet domestic demand," the sugar body said.
"In the short term then, stocks will continue to be held by private millers...Exporters are likely to export small volumes of sugar for short term expediency in response to mounting storage costs."

Private traders and millers in India, the world's largest sugar cane producer and the second largest sugar producing and consuming nation, have been allowed to export since January. Before that all exports were done by the state.

The ISO said that the deregulatory move had in fact resulted in lower exports in the 1996/97 season (Oct-Sept) -- analysts export them to total only 400,000 tonnes -- than previously allowed for under the government quota system.

This was partly due to millers' reluctance to export to the world market, where prices are typically less than Indian production costs. When government ran all exports, losses were shared on a pro-rata basis by the mills.
Only a significant increase in world prices was likely to tempt Indian sugar players to send product offshore.

Czarnikow Sugar earlier this month cut its estimate for India's 1996/97 sugar output to 14.24 million tonnes raw value, down 760,000 tonnes on its previous forecast. It also noted industry expectations of an even lower crop in 1997/98.
India produced a bumper 17.88 million tonne harvest in 1995/96.
